title: NAT
body:
Network Address Translation is what lets an entire household of devices share a single public [[IP Address]]. Each device gets a private address (`192.168.x.x`, `10.x.x.x`) assigned by your router, meaningful only inside your own network. On the way out, the router rewrites the source address to the one public IP your household presents to the internet, and records the mapping in a translation table so that replies can be routed back to the correct device and port inside your home.

NAT is a large part of why IPv4 exhaustion hasn't been fatal — billions of devices hide behind a much smaller number of public addresses. It's also why an inbound connection to a device on your home network doesn't "just work": nothing in the translation table tells the router which device the unsolicited packet was for, which is what port forwarding exists to solve.
